title: French 1
description: Free French 1 study guide: 8 units, 320 practice questions, 80 flashcards, quick reference, memory tricks, and a full practice exam. Completely free.

units.name: Greetings & Alphabet

concepts.intro: French greetings change with time of day and formality. Getting the right register matters as much as the words themselves.
b: Bonjour = hello/good day (used until evening); Bonsoir = good evening
Salut = hi/bye (informal, use with friends and family only)
Au revoir = goodbye (all situations); À bientôt = see you soon; À demain = see you tomorrow
Comment allez-vous ? (formal) vs Comment vas-tu ? / Ça va ? (informal) = How are you?
Ça va bien, merci = I'm doing well, thanks; Comme ci, comme ça = so-so
Enchanté(e) = pleased to meet you, used right after an introduction

concepts.intro: French has two words for 'you', and choosing the wrong one is a real social error, not just a grammar point.
b: Tu = informal 'you', singular — family, friends, children, peers
Vous = formal 'you' singular (strangers, elders, authority) AND always plural 'you'
When in doubt with an adult stranger, use vous
Vous is also used for a group even if all members are close friends
Switching from vous to tu (se tutoyer) usually happens by mutual invitation

concepts.intro: The French alphabet has the same 26 letters as English but they are pronounced differently, which matters for spelling names aloud.
b: A (ah), B (bé), C (sé), D (dé), E (euh), F (ef), G (jé)
H (ash) — always silent at the start of a word, e.g. 'hôtel'
I (i), J (ji), K (ka), L (el), M (em), N (en)
O (o), P (pé), Q (ku), R (er), S (es), T (té)
U (u), V (vé), W (double-vé), X (iks), Y (i grec), Z (zed)

concepts.intro: Accents are not decorative — they change pronunciation and sometimes meaning, and must be written correctly.
b: é = accent aigu (closed 'ay' sound), e.g. café, étudiant
è / ê = accent grave / circonflexe (open 'eh' sound), e.g. mère, fête
ç = cédille, makes 'c' sound like 's' before a, o, u — e.g. ça, français
ë / ï = tréma, shows two vowels are pronounced separately, e.g. Noël
a vs à: 'a' = has (from avoir); 'à' = to/at — the accent changes the meaning

concepts.intro: Numbers 0–20 are used constantly for ages, phone numbers, and quantities and must be memorized as irregular forms.
b: 0 zéro, 1 un, 2 deux, 3 trois, 4 quatre, 5 cinq
6 six, 7 sept, 8 huit, 9 neuf, 10 dix
11 onze, 12 douze, 13 treize, 14 quatorze, 15 quinze
16 seize, 17 dix-sept, 18 dix-huit, 19 dix-neuf, 20 vingt
Final consonants of six, huit, dix are often dropped before a consonant sound (six livres → 'si livres')

keyFacts: Bonjour is used any time until evening; switch to bonsoir once it gets dark.
Vous is required for strangers/authority and is always used for groups, regardless of familiarity.
The letter h is always silent in French, so 'les hôtels' liaisons as if h weren't there.
Accents change pronunciation and meaning (a vs à, ou vs où) — never optional in spelling.
traps: Salut to a teacher or stranger, not Bonjour — Salut is informal and can sound rude to someone you don't know.
'Comment tu t'appelles' with vous — mixing tu and vous in the same sentence is inconsistent; pick one register.
Dropping accents when typing (cafe instead of café) changes correctness on exams even if pronunciation seems similar.
Pronouncing the h in 'huit' or 'hôtel' — French h is silent, not aspirated like English h.

units.name: Articles & Nouns

concepts.intro: Every French noun is either masculine or feminine, even for objects with no natural gender, and this must be memorized with each word.
b: le livre (m) = the book; la table (f) = the table — gender is arbitrary for objects
Nouns ending in -e are often (not always) feminine: la chaise, la porte
Nouns ending in -tion, -sion, -té are almost always feminine: la nation, la liberté
Nouns ending in -eau, -age, -isme are usually masculine: le bureau, le fromage
Always learn a noun WITH its article (le/la) rather than the noun alone

concepts.l: Definite Articles: le, la, l', les
concepts.intro: Definite articles ('the') agree in gender and number with the noun and contract before vowel sounds.
b: le = masculine singular: le garçon, le stylo
la = feminine singular: la fille, la maison
l' = before any singular noun starting with a vowel or mute h: l'ami, l'homme
les = plural for both genders: les garçons, les filles
Definite articles are used for specific things, general categories, and likes/dislikes (j'aime les chats)

concepts.intro: Indefinite articles ('a/an/some') introduce a non-specific noun and also agree in gender and number.
b: un = a/an (masculine): un livre, un stylo
une = a/an (feminine): une table, une pomme
des = some (plural, both genders): des livres, des pommes
In negative sentences, un/une/des become 'de' (or 'd'' before a vowel): j'ai un chien → je n'ai pas de chien
Des is often omitted in English ('I have books') but is required in French (j'ai des livres)

concepts.intro: Most French nouns form the plural by adding -s, but common exceptions must be memorized.
b: Regular: le livre → les livres (add -s, usually silent)
Nouns ending in -s, -x, -z stay the same: le fils → les fils; la voix → les voix
Nouns ending in -eau, -eu add -x: le bureau → les bureaux; le jeu → les jeux
Most nouns ending in -al change to -aux: le journal → les journaux
The article changes to show plural even when the noun's sound doesn't: le chat → les chats

concepts.intro: The prepositions à (to/at) and de (of/from) contract with the masculine and plural definite articles.
b: à + le = au: je vais au cinéma (not 'à le')
à + les = aux: je parle aux étudiants
de + le = du: le livre du professeur (not 'de le')
de + les = des: la voiture des parents
à + la and à + l' do NOT contract: à la piscine, à l'école

keyFacts: Every noun has a gender (masculine or feminine) that must be memorized along with the word itself.
Articles agree in gender and number: le/la/les and un/une/des.
à + le → au and de + le → du are required contractions; à la, à l', de la, de l' never contract.
After a negation, un/une/des become de/d' (except after être).
traps: 'la programme' instead of 'le programme' — memorize gender per word, don't guess from English logic.
Saying 'à le cinéma' instead of 'au cinéma' — à+le must contract to au.
Forgetting 'des' in 'j'ai des amis' — English drops the article, French keeps it.
Using un/une after a negation ('je n'ai pas un stylo') instead of de: 'je n'ai pas de stylo'.

units.name: Regular -ER Verbs

concepts.intro: Over 90% of French verbs end in -er in the infinitive and follow one predictable conjugation pattern.
b: parler (to speak), aimer (to like/love), habiter (to live), travailler (to work)
manger (to eat), regarder (to watch/look at), écouter (to listen), donner (to give)
chercher (to look for), jouer (to play), étudier (to study), arriver (to arrive)
To conjugate: remove -er from the infinitive to get the stem (parl-, aim-)
Add the ending that matches the subject pronoun to the stem

concepts.intro: The six present-tense endings for -er verbs attach to the stem and must be memorized as a set.
b: je parle, tu parles, il/elle/on parle (endings -e, -es, -e all sound the same)
nous parlons, vous parlez, ils/elles parlent
-ent (ils/elles) is silent — 'ils parlent' sounds just like 'il parle'
-ons (nous) and -ez (vous) are the only endings that are clearly pronounced
je → j' before a vowel sound: j'aime, j'habite, j'écoute

concepts.intro: To make a verb negative, French wraps it in two parts placed around the conjugated verb.
b: ne + verb + pas: je ne parle pas (I do not speak)
ne becomes n' before a vowel sound: je n'aime pas, il n'habite pas
Both ne and pas are required — dropping ne is only acceptable in very casual spoken French
Other negations follow the same pattern: ne...jamais (never), ne...plus (no longer)
Word order: subject + ne + verb + pas + rest of sentence

concepts.intro: A few common -er verbs need a small spelling tweak in certain forms to preserve pronunciation.
b: manger (to eat) adds an -e before -ons: nous mangeons (keeps the soft 'j' sound)
commencer (to begin) changes c to ç before -ons: nous commençons
acheter (to buy) adds a grave accent in most forms: j'achète, but nous achetons
préférer (to prefer) changes é to è in most forms: je préfère, but nous préférons
appeler (to call) doubles the l in most forms: j'appelle, but nous appelons

concepts.intro: The present tense in French covers more ground than in English, including some ongoing and near-future actions.
b: Je parle can mean 'I speak', 'I am speaking', or 'I do speak' — one form, three English meanings
aujourd'hui (today), maintenant (now), souvent (often), toujours (always)
adorer (to adore) and détester (to hate) follow the same -er pattern
aimer + infinitive: j'aime danser (I like to dance)
Adverbs like souvent/toujours usually go right after the conjugated verb: je mange souvent

keyFacts: -er verbs share one pattern: stem + -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent.
The ils/elles ending -ent is silent, so nous/vous forms carry the audible distinction.
Negation surrounds the verb: ne (n') + verb + pas.
manger, commencer, acheter, préférer, appeler need small spelling adjustments to keep their sound.
traps: Pronouncing the -ent ending in 'ils parlent' — it is silent, don't add a syllable.
'Je ne aime pas' instead of 'je n'aime pas' — ne must elide to n' before a vowel.
'Nous mangons' instead of 'nous mangeons' — manger needs the extra e to keep the soft g sound.
Using the infinitive alone as a conjugated verb ('je parler') instead of conjugating: 'je parle'.

units.name: Être, Avoir & Questions

concepts.intro: Être is the most important irregular verb in French, used for identity, description, nationality, and profession.
b: je suis, tu es, il/elle/on est
nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont
Used for adjectives of description: elle est grande (she is tall)
Used for professions and nationalities without an article: il est professeur, elle est française
C'est vs il/elle est: c'est + noun (c'est un professeur), il/elle est + adjective alone (il est intelligent)

concepts.intro: Avoir is the second essential irregular verb, used for possession and many fixed expressions where English uses 'to be'.
b: j'ai, tu as, il/elle/on a
nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont
Possession: j'ai un chat (I have a cat)
Age: j'ai vingt ans (I am twenty — literally 'I have twenty years')
Fixed expressions: avoir faim (to be hungry), avoir soif (to be thirsty), avoir chaud/froid (to be hot/cold), avoir peur (to be afraid)

concepts.intro: Il y a is an invariable expression meaning 'there is/there are', built from il + y + a (from avoir).
b: Il y a un livre sur la table = There is a book on the table
Il y a des étudiants dans la salle = There are students in the room
Never changes form regardless of singular or plural: always 'il y a', never 'ils y ont'
Negative: il n'y a pas de + noun (il n'y a pas de pain = there isn't any bread)
Question form: Y a-t-il...? or Est-ce qu'il y a...?

concepts.intro: French has three ways to ask a yes/no question, ranging from casual to formal.
b: Rising intonation (informal, spoken): Tu parles français ? (just raise your voice at the end)
Est-ce que + statement (neutral, common): Est-ce que tu parles français ?
Inversion (formal/written): Parles-tu français ? (verb and subject pronoun swap, joined by a hyphen)
With a name/noun subject, inversion adds a pronoun: Marie parle-t-elle français ?
A -t- is inserted between two vowels in inversion: Parle-t-il ? (not 'Parle-il')

concepts.intro: Question words replace the missing information and usually come first in the sentence.
b: Qui = who: Qui est-ce ? (Who is it?)
Que/Qu'est-ce que = what: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ? (What are you doing?)
Où = where: Où habites-tu ?
Quand = when; Pourquoi = why; Comment = how; Combien (de) = how much/many
Quel(le)(s) = which/what, agrees with the noun: Quelle heure est-il ? (What time is it?)

keyFacts: Être and avoir are irregular and must be memorized separately from -er verb patterns.
Avoir is used where English uses 'to be' for age and physical states (faim, soif, chaud, froid, peur).
Il y a is invariable — it never agrees with what follows.
Question words (qui, que, où, quand, pourquoi, comment) go at the start of the sentence.
traps: 'Je suis 20 ans' instead of 'j'ai 20 ans' — age uses avoir, not être.
'Il est un professeur' instead of 'il est professeur' or 'c'est un professeur' — no article after il/elle est + profession.
'Ils y ont des livres' instead of 'il y a des livres' — il y a never conjugates to agree with the noun.
Forgetting the -t- in inversion: 'Parle-il' instead of 'Parle-t-il'.

units.name: Adjectives & Description

concepts.intro: French adjectives must match the gender of the noun they describe, usually by adding -e for the feminine form.
b: Regular pattern: add -e for feminine — grand → grande, petit → petite, intelligent → intelligente
Adjectives already ending in -e don't change: un homme rouge → une femme rouge
-eux → -euse: heureux → heureuse (happy); -f → -ve: actif → active
-on/-en double the consonant + e: bon → bonne, italien → italienne
Some are irregular and must be memorized: beau → belle, nouveau → nouvelle, vieux → vieille

concepts.intro: Adjectives also agree in number, usually by adding -s for the plural, on top of gender agreement.
b: Regular: grand → grands (m. pl.), grande → grandes (f. pl.)
Adjectives ending in -s or -x don't change in the masculine plural: un garçon français → des garçons français
-eau → -eaux in the masculine plural: un beau tableau → de beaux tableaux
Agreement is four-way: masc. sing., fem. sing., masc. pl., fem. pl. (petit, petite, petits, petites)
A mixed-gender group of nouns takes the masculine plural adjective

concepts.intro: Most French adjectives follow the noun, but a short list of common ones come before it — this must be memorized.
b: Most descriptive adjectives follow the noun: une voiture rouge, un livre intéressant
BAGS adjectives come before the noun: Beauty, Age, Goodness, Size
Beauty/Goodness: beau (beautiful), joli (pretty), bon (good), mauvais (bad)
Age/Size: jeune (young), vieux (old), nouveau (new), grand (big/tall), petit (small), gros (fat)
Examples: une belle maison, un jeune homme, un bon livre, une petite table

concepts.intro: French uses two different structures to say 'he/she/it is' depending on what follows.
b: C'est + article + noun: c'est un livre, c'est une bonne idée
C'est + adjective (general comment): c'est intéressant, c'est difficile
Il/Elle est + adjective alone (describing a specific person/thing already mentioned): elle est grande
Il/Elle est + profession/nationality (no article): il est médecin, elle est canadienne
Ce sont (plural of c'est) + noun: ce sont mes amis

concepts.intro: A core set of adjectives lets you describe people, places, and things in almost any conversation.
b: grand/grande (tall/big), petit/petite (small), beau/belle (beautiful), joli/jolie (pretty)
intelligent(e), sympathique (nice/friendly), gentil/gentille (kind), drôle (funny)
content(e) (happy), triste (sad), fatigué(e) (tired), occupé(e) (busy)
difficile (difficult), facile (easy), intéressant(e), ennuyeux/ennuyeuse (boring)
Colors as adjectives agree too: une chemise bleue, des chaussures noires

keyFacts: Adjectives agree with the noun in both gender and number, giving four possible forms.
Most adjectives follow the noun; BAGS adjectives (Beauty, Age, Goodness, Size) precede it.
C'est is followed by an article + noun; il/elle est drops the article for professions/nationalities.
Beau, nouveau, and vieux have a special form before a masculine noun starting with a vowel: bel, nouvel, vieil.
traps: 'une voiture rouges' instead of 'une voiture rouge' — don't add -s just because it 'sounds descriptive'; agreement is grammatical, not decorative.
'un maison grand' instead of 'une grande maison' — grand is a BAGS adjective and must go before the noun.
'Il est un docteur' instead of 'il est docteur' or 'c'est un docteur' — mixing the two structures.
Forgetting irregular feminine forms: 'une belle' is correct but 'un beau homme' is wrong — it must be 'un bel homme' before a vowel sound.

units.name: Family & Possession

concepts.intro: Family vocabulary is essential for talking about yourself and is tested constantly with possessive adjectives.
b: le père (father), la mère (mother), les parents (parents)
le frère (brother), la sœur (sister), le/la enfant (child)
le fils (son), la fille (daughter/girl — context tells you which)
le mari (husband), la femme (wife/woman — context tells you which)
les grands-parents, le grand-père, la grand-mère

concepts.intro: Extended family terms build naturally from the immediate family words using compound patterns.
b: l'oncle (uncle), la tante (aunt)
le cousin, la cousine (cousin)
le neveu (nephew), la nièce (niece)
le beau-père (father-in-law/stepfather), la belle-mère (mother-in-law/stepmother)
les petits-enfants (grandchildren), le petit-fils (grandson), la petite-fille (granddaughter)

concepts.intro: Possessive adjectives agree with the noun they describe (the thing owned), not with the owner's gender.
b: mon/ma/mes = my: mon père, ma mère, mes parents
ton/ta/tes = your (informal): ton frère, ta sœur, tes enfants
The form depends on the GENDER OF THE NOUN, not the speaker: 'my mother' is 'ma mère' regardless of who's speaking
mon (not ma) is used before a feminine noun starting with a vowel sound: mon amie (not 'ma amie')
Plural mes/tes is used for any plural noun regardless of gender

concepts.intro: The remaining possessive adjectives cover his/her, our, your (formal/plural), and their.
b: son/sa/ses = his/her/its — again agrees with the noun owned, not the owner's gender: son père can mean 'his father' OR 'her father'
notre/nos = our: notre maison, nos enfants (only two forms: singular and plural)
votre/vos = your (formal or plural): votre travail, vos amis
leur/leurs = their: leur chat, leurs chats
son ami (his/her friend, masc.) vs sa amie is wrong — use son amie before a feminine vowel-starting noun

concepts.intro: Besides possessive adjectives, French shows ownership with 'de' + noun, since it has no apostrophe-s like English.
b: le livre de Marie = Marie's book (literally 'the book of Marie')
la voiture de mon père = my father's car
de + le = du, de + les = des (contractions still apply): le chien du voisin (the neighbor's dog)
There is no French equivalent of 's — always restructure with de
C'est le sac de qui ? = Whose bag is it?

keyFacts: Possessive adjectives (mon/ton/son etc.) agree with the noun possessed, not with the possessor's gender.
Son/sa/ses can mean his OR her — context clarifies which.
French has no possessive 's; use noun + de + owner instead.
Mon/ton/son replace ma/ta/sa before a feminine noun starting with a vowel sound (mon amie, ton école).
traps: 'Sa mère' assumed to mean only 'her mother' — it can equally mean 'his mother'; only context tells you.
'Ma amie' instead of 'mon amie' — before a feminine vowel-starting noun, use mon even though the noun is feminine.
Writing 'Marie's book' as 'Marie's livre' — French has no apostrophe-s; say 'le livre de Marie'.
Confusing 'la fille' (daughter/girl) meaning based on missing context, and 'le fils' (son) — don't mix them up as gender pairs of the same word.

units.name: Food & Café Culture

concepts.intro: Core food vocabulary lets you order, shop, and talk about meals — a high-frequency beginner topic.
b: le pain (bread), le fromage (cheese), les œufs (eggs), la viande (meat)
les légumes (vegetables), les fruits (fruit), le poisson (fish)
l'eau (water), le café (coffee), le thé (tea), le jus d'orange (orange juice), le vin (wine)
le petit-déjeuner (breakfast), le déjeuner (lunch), le dîner (dinner)
sucré (sweet), salé (salty/savory), délicieux/délicieuse (delicious)

concepts.l: The Partitive Article: du, de la, de l', des
concepts.intro: The partitive article expresses 'some' of an uncountable or unspecified quantity, and is required where English often omits it.
b: du + masculine noun: je mange du pain (I eat/am eating some bread)
de la + feminine noun: je bois de la limonade
de l' + vowel-starting noun: je voudrais de l'eau
des + plural noun: je mange des légumes
In a negative sentence, all partitives become de/d': je ne mange pas de viande

concepts.intro: Vouloir (to want) is irregular and its conditional form 'voudrais' is the standard polite way to order or request something.
b: je veux, tu veux, il/elle/on veut, nous voulons, vous voulez, ils/elles veulent
Je voudrais... = I would like... (more polite than je veux for ordering)
Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît = I would like a coffee, please
vouloir + infinitive: je veux manger (I want to eat)
s'il vous plaît (formal) vs s'il te plaît (informal) = please

concepts.intro: Café culture is central to French daily life, and ordering food/drink follows set polite phrases.
b: Qu'est-ce que vous prenez ? = What will you have? (server's question)
Je prends un café crème = I'll have a coffee with cream (prendre = to take/have food)
L'addition, s'il vous plaît = The check, please
C'est combien ? / Ça coûte combien ? = How much is it?
un croissant, une baguette, un sandwich, une tarte, une crêpe are classic café/bakery items

concepts.intro: Talking about food naturally involves the avoir expressions for hunger/thirst and verbs of preference.
b: avoir faim (to be hungry), avoir soif (to be thirsty)
préférer + noun/infinitive: je préfère le thé (I prefer tea)
aimer/adorer/détester + le/la/les + food: j'adore le chocolat, je déteste les épinards
Manger and boire are the key verbs: manger (to eat, regular -er) and boire (to drink, irregular: je bois, nous buvons)
au restaurant, au café, à la boulangerie (à + la = à la, no contraction) are common location phrases

keyFacts: The partitive article (du/de la/de l'/des) means 'some' and is required with food/drink even when English omits it.
In negative sentences, du/de la/des collapse to de/d'.
Je voudrais is the polite conditional form used for ordering, more courteous than je veux.
Boire (to drink) is irregular: je bois, nous buvons, ils boivent.
traps: 'Je mange pain' instead of 'je mange du pain' — the partitive article can't be dropped as it can in English.
'Je veux un café' at a counter instead of the more polite 'je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît'.
'Je ne mange pas du fromage' instead of 'je ne mange pas de fromage' — partitive becomes de after negation.
Confusing manger (to eat) with the false-friend-sounding 'manager' — manger is a regular -er verb, not related in meaning.

units.name: City Places & Directions

concepts.intro: Naming common locations lets you talk about your daily routine and ask for or give directions.
b: la banque (bank), la boulangerie (bakery), la pharmacie (pharmacy), le supermarché (supermarket)
la gare (train station), l'aéroport (airport), l'hôpital (hospital), l'école (school)
le musée (museum), l'église (church), la bibliothèque (library), le parc (park)
la poste (post office), le marché (market), la place (square), la rue (street)
le magasin (store), le cinéma (movie theater), la piscine (pool)

concepts.intro: Aller is the essential irregular verb for movement and combines with à + place to say where someone is going.
b: je vais, tu vas, il/elle/on va, nous allons, vous allez, ils/elles vont
aller + à + le = aller au: je vais au parc, je vais au musée
aller + à + la (no contraction): je vais à la banque, je vais à la piscine
aller + à + l' (no contraction, vowel start): je vais à l'école, je vais à l'hôpital
aller + à + les = aller aux: je vais aux toilettes

concepts.intro: Prepositions of place describe exactly where something is relative to another location, essential for directions.
b: à côté de (next to), en face de (across from), près de (near), loin de (far from)
devant (in front of), derrière (behind), entre (between), sur (on), sous (under), dans (in/inside)
à droite (to/on the right), à gauche (to/on the left), tout droit (straight ahead)
à côté de + le = à côté du; près de + les = près des (de contracts here too)
au coin de (at/on the corner of): au coin de la rue

concepts.intro: Direction-giving uses the imperative mood and a compact set of fixed phrases every beginner should know.
b: Où est... ? / Où se trouve... ? = Where is...?
Pour aller à..., s'il vous plaît ? = How do I get to..., please?
Imperative forms: tournez (turn, vous-form), continuez (continue), prenez (take)
Tournez à droite / Tournez à gauche = Turn right / Turn left
Continuez tout droit jusqu'à... = Continue straight until...

concepts.intro: Rounding out city vocabulary means being able to say how far something is and how you get there.
b: C'est loin ? / C'est près d'ici ? = Is it far? / Is it near here?
à pied (on foot), en bus (by bus), en voiture (by car), en métro (by subway), à vélo (by bike)
à + distance: c'est à cinq minutes (it's five minutes away)
prendre + transportation: je prends le métro (I take the subway)
Il faut + infinitive = it's necessary to / you have to: il faut tourner à gauche

keyFacts: Aller is irregular (vais/vas/va/allons/allez/vont) and combines with à for destinations.
à + le → au and à + les → aux, but à + la and à + l' never contract.
de-based prepositions (à côté de, près de, en face de) also contract: à côté du parc, près des magasins.
Direction-giving uses the vous-form imperative: tournez, continuez, prenez.
traps: 'Je vais à le musée' instead of 'je vais au musée' — à+le must contract to au.
'à côté de le parc' instead of 'à côté du parc' — de+le contracts to du even inside longer prepositions.
Confusing à droite (to the right) with the adjective droit/droite (straight/right-hand) — tout droit means 'straight ahead', not 'all right'.
Using tu-form imperative (tourne) with a stranger when giving directions — use the vous-form (tournez) by default.

quiz.q: Which greeting is appropriate any time before evening?
quiz.e: Bonjour is used from morning until evening; Bonsoir replaces it after dark.

quiz.q: Which word should you avoid using with a stranger or authority figure?
quiz.e: Salut is informal (hi/bye) and should be reserved for friends and family.

quiz.q: What does 'Enchanté(e)' mean?
quiz.e: Enchanté(e) is said right after being introduced to someone.

quiz.q: Which pronoun must you use for a group of people, even close friends?
quiz.e: Vous is always used for plural 'you', regardless of familiarity.

quiz.q: When should you use 'tu' instead of 'vous'?
o: With a stranger on the street
With a close friend or family member
With an elderly person you just met
quiz.e: Tu is reserved for informal relationships: friends, family, peers, children.

quiz.q: How do you say 'see you tomorrow'?
quiz.e: À demain literally means 'until tomorrow'.

quiz.q: What is the correct response to 'Comment allez-vous ?'
quiz.e: Ça va bien, merci answers how you are doing.

quiz.q: Which letter is always silent at the start of a French word?
quiz.e: The letter h is always silent in French, as in 'hôtel'.

quiz.q: How is the letter 'C' pronounced in the French alphabet?
quiz.e: C is pronounced 'sé' in French.

quiz.q: What is the French name for the letter 'W'?
quiz.e: W is called 'double-vé' in French.

quiz.q: What does the cédille (ç) do to the letter c?
o: Makes it sound like 's' before a, o, u
quiz.e: The cédille makes c sound like 's' before a, o, or u, as in 'ça' or 'français'.

quiz.q: What is the difference between 'a' and 'à'?
quiz.e: 'a' comes from avoir (has); 'à' is the preposition meaning to/at.

quiz.q: Which accent appears in 'mère' and 'fête'?
quiz.e: È and ê both give an open 'eh' sound; mère uses è, fête uses ê.

quiz.q: What does the tréma (¨) indicate, as in 'Noël'?
quiz.e: The tréma shows that two adjacent vowels are pronounced as separate sounds.

quiz.q: How do you write the number 15 in French?
quiz.e: 15 = quinze.

quiz.q: How do you write the number 17 in French?
quiz.e: 17 = dix-sept (literally 'ten-seven').

quiz.q: What number is 'vingt'?
quiz.e: Vingt = 20.

quiz.q: What is the correct spelling of the number 11?
quiz.e: 11 = onze.

quiz.q: Which of these numbers often drops its final consonant before another consonant sound?
quiz.e: Six often drops its final 's' sound before a consonant, e.g. 'six livres'.

quiz.q: How do you say 'good evening' in French?
quiz.e: Bonsoir means good evening, used once it gets dark.

quiz.q: 'Comme ci, comme ça' means:
quiz.e: Comme ci, comme ça expresses a neutral, so-so feeling.

quiz.q: Which is the informal way to ask 'how are you'?
quiz.e: Ça va ? is the casual, informal way to ask how someone is doing.

quiz.q: What is the correct pronunciation focus for 'huit'?
quiz.e: French h is always silent, including in huit (eight).

quiz.q: Which word means 'goodbye' and works in any situation?
quiz.e: Au revoir is the universally appropriate way to say goodbye.

quiz.q: What does 'é' sound like compared to 'è'?
o: é is open, è is closed
é is closed, è is open
quiz.e: É (accent aigu) is a closed sound; è (accent grave) is more open.

quiz.q: How do you spell your name using the French alphabet if it contains a 'J'?
quiz.e: J is pronounced 'ji' in the French alphabet.

quiz.q: Which number is 'quatorze'?
quiz.e: Quatorze = 14.

quiz.q: Which greeting would be too casual for meeting your professor for the first time?
quiz.e: Salut is too informal for a first meeting with an authority figure.

quiz.q: What does 'à bientôt' mean?
quiz.e: À bientôt = see you soon.

quiz.q: Select the correctly accented word.
quiz.e: The correct spelling with accent aigu is café.

quiz.q: Which pronunciation rule applies to 'dix' before a vowel-starting word?
o: The x can sound like 'z' in liaison
There is no x sound ever
quiz.e: In liaison, the x in dix can be pronounced like a 'z' sound before a vowel, e.g. 'dix ans'.

quiz.q: What is the plural courtesy title equivalent, used to address a married woman formally?
quiz.e: Madame is the formal title for an adult woman, especially if married.

quiz.q: Which of these numbers is irregular in a way you must simply memorize (not built from smaller numbers)?
quiz.e: Seize (16) is a standalone form, unlike dix-sept/dix-huit/dix-neuf which are visibly 'ten + unit'.

quiz.q: 'Au revoir' is best translated as:
quiz.e: Au revoir literally suggests 'until we see each other again'.

quiz.q: What is the correct French letter name for 'G'?
quiz.e: G is pronounced 'jé' in French.

quiz.q: Which is the correct order for numbers 0-3?
quiz.e: The correct sequence is zéro, un, deux, trois.

quiz.q: What is a safe default choice of 'you' when speaking to an adult you've just met?
quiz.e: Vous is the safe, respectful default with someone you don't know well.

quiz.q: Which of the following words needs a cédille to keep its 's' sound?
quiz.e: Both garçon and français need the cédille (ç) to preserve the 's' sound before a, o.

quiz.q: How would you greet someone you know well in a casual setting?
quiz.e: Salut is perfect for informal greetings among friends.

quiz.q: What is the correct definite article for 'livre' (book, masculine)?
quiz.e: Le is the masculine singular definite article: le livre.

quiz.q: What is the correct definite article for 'maison' (house, feminine)?
quiz.e: La is the feminine singular definite article: la maison.

quiz.q: Which article is used before 'ami' (a vowel-starting noun)?
quiz.e: L' replaces le/la before any singular noun starting with a vowel or mute h.

quiz.q: What is the plural definite article for both genders?
quiz.e: Les is used for all plural nouns, regardless of gender.

quiz.q: Which nouns are usually feminine based on their ending?
quiz.e: Nouns ending in -tion are almost always feminine, e.g. la nation.

quiz.q: Which nouns are usually masculine based on their ending?
quiz.e: Nouns ending in -eau are usually masculine, e.g. le bureau.

quiz.q: What is the correct indefinite article for 'stylo' (pen, masculine)?
quiz.e: Un is the masculine singular indefinite article.

quiz.q: What is the correct indefinite article for 'pomme' (apple, feminine)?
quiz.e: Une is the feminine singular indefinite article.

quiz.q: What is the plural indefinite article?
quiz.e: Des means 'some' and is used for plural nouns of either gender.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I have some books' correctly in French?
quiz.e: French requires the article 'des' even though English can drop 'some'.

quiz.q: What happens to 'un/une/des' in a negative sentence?
quiz.e: After a negation, indefinite/partitive articles become de/d': je n'ai pas de chien.

quiz.q: How do you form the plural of 'le livre'?
quiz.e: Add -s to the noun and change the article to les: les livres.

quiz.q: What is the plural of 'le fils' (son)?
quiz.e: Nouns already ending in -s don't change in the plural: le fils → les fils.

quiz.q: What is the plural of 'le bureau' (desk)?
quiz.e: Nouns ending in -eau add -x in the plural: les bureaux.

quiz.q: What is the plural of 'le journal' (newspaper)?
quiz.e: Most -al nouns change to -aux in the plural: les journaux.

quiz.q: What is the correct contraction for 'à + le'?
quiz.e: À + le always contracts to au: je vais au cinéma.

quiz.q: What is the correct contraction for 'à + les'?
quiz.e: À + les contracts to aux: je parle aux étudiants.

quiz.q: What is the correct contraction for 'de + le'?
quiz.e: De + le contracts to du: le livre du professeur.

quiz.q: What is the correct contraction for 'de + les'?
quiz.e: De + les contracts to des: la voiture des parents.

quiz.q: Does 'à + la' contract?
quiz.e: À la and à l' never contract, unlike à le and à les.

quiz.q: Choose the correctly gendered noun phrase.
quiz.e: Programme is masculine: le programme.

quiz.q: Which is the best strategy for learning noun gender?
o: Memorize the noun with its article
Assume all abstract nouns are feminine
quiz.e: Always learn a noun together with its article (le/la) since gender is often arbitrary.

quiz.q: How do you say 'a friend' if 'ami' begins with a vowel and is masculine?
quiz.e: Un ami is correct; the vowel affects 'le/la→l'' for definite articles, but un/une don't elide.

quiz.q: What is the definite article for 'hôtel' (masculine, starts with mute h)?
quiz.e: L' is used because h is silent and hôtel starts with a vowel sound.

quiz.q: Which sentence correctly uses the negative form of an indefinite article?
quiz.e: After a negation, un/une/des become de: je n'ai pas de stylo.

quiz.q: What is the plural of 'le jeu' (game)?
quiz.e: Nouns ending in -eu typically add -x in the plural: les jeux.

quiz.q: Which noun ending strongly suggests feminine gender?
quiz.e: Nouns ending in -té are almost always feminine, e.g. la liberté.

quiz.q: Complete: 'Je vais ___ cinéma.'
quiz.e: À + le contracts to au before a masculine noun.

quiz.q: Complete: 'Je vais ___ piscine.'
quiz.e: À la is used before a feminine noun and does not contract.

quiz.q: Complete: 'C'est le livre ___ professeur.'
quiz.e: De + le contracts to du.

quiz.q: Complete: 'La voiture ___ parents.'
quiz.e: De + les contracts to des.

quiz.q: Which article set correctly matches 'des livres intéressants' meaning?
quiz.e: Des is the plural indefinite article, meaning 'some'.

quiz.q: Why is 'des' often mistakenly omitted by English speakers?
o: Because French never uses plural articles
Because English drops 'some' but French keeps 'des'
Because des is optional in French
Because des only applies to feminine nouns
quiz.e: English can say 'I have books' without an article, but French requires 'j'ai des livres'.

quiz.q: What gender is 'la liberté'?
quiz.e: La liberté is feminine, consistent with the -té ending pattern.

quiz.q: What gender is 'le fromage'?
quiz.e: Le fromage is masculine, consistent with the -age ending pattern.

quiz.q: Which definite article is used with 'école' (feminine, vowel-starting)?
quiz.e: L' replaces la before a vowel-starting noun.

quiz.q: Choose the correct plural: 'la voix' (voice) →
quiz.e: Nouns ending in -x stay the same in the plural: la voix → les voix.

quiz.q: What is the rule for indefinite articles after être in the negative?
o: They do NOT change to de
quiz.e: Unlike other verbs, ce n'est pas un/une stays un/une after être in the negative.

quiz.q: Which is correct: 'un ami' or 'un amie'?
quiz.e: Amie is the feminine spelling (une amie); the masculine is ami (un ami).

quiz.q: Select the correct plural definite article usage: 'les chats'
quiz.e: Les chats = the cats (plural definite).

quiz.q: What is the infinitive ending shared by the majority of French verbs?
quiz.e: Over 90% of French verbs are regular -er verbs like parler and aimer.

quiz.q: What is the correct 'je' form of 'parler'?
quiz.e: Je parle — remove -er, add -e for je.

quiz.q: What is the correct 'nous' form of 'parler'?
quiz.e: Nous parlons — the nous ending is -ons.

quiz.q: What is the correct 'ils' form of 'aimer'?
quiz.e: Ils/elles aiment — the ending -ent is silent.

quiz.q: What is the correct 'tu' form of 'habiter'?
quiz.e: Tu habites — the tu ending is -es.

quiz.q: Which ending is silent when spoken?
quiz.e: The -ent ending for ils/elles is silent; 'ils parlent' sounds like 'il parle'.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I love' before a vowel-starting verb stem?
quiz.e: Je elides to j' before a vowel sound: j'aime.

quiz.q: What is the negative form of 'je parle'?
quiz.e: Negation wraps the verb: ne + verb + pas.

quiz.q: How do you say 'he doesn't like' correctly?
quiz.e: Ne elides to n' before a vowel: il n'aime pas.

quiz.q: What is the correct nous form of 'manger'?
quiz.e: Manger adds an extra -e before -ons to keep the soft g sound: nous mangeons.

quiz.q: What is the correct nous form of 'commencer'?
quiz.e: Commencer changes c to ç before -ons to keep the soft sound: nous commençons.

quiz.q: What is the correct je form of 'acheter'?
quiz.e: Acheter takes a grave accent in most forms except nous/vous: j'achète.

quiz.q: What is the correct nous form of 'acheter'?
quiz.e: Nous and vous forms of acheter keep the unaccented stem: nous achetons.

quiz.q: What is the correct je form of 'préférer'?
quiz.e: Préférer changes é to è in most forms: je préfère.

quiz.q: What is the correct nous form of 'préférer'?
quiz.e: Nous préférons keeps the é, unlike je/tu/il/ils forms.

quiz.q: What is the correct je form of 'appeler'?
quiz.e: Appeler doubles the l in most forms: j'appelle.

quiz.q: What three English meanings can 'je parle' express?
quiz.e: French present tense covers simple, progressive, and emphatic meanings in English.

quiz.q: Where does an adverb like 'souvent' usually go?
quiz.e: Adverbs like souvent/toujours typically follow the conjugated verb: je mange souvent.

quiz.q: Which is the correct infinitive-to-stem process?
o: Remove -er from the infinitive to get the stem
quiz.e: Remove -er from the infinitive (parler → parl-) to get the stem for conjugation.

quiz.q: What does 'chercher' mean?
quiz.e: Chercher means 'to look for/search for'.

quiz.q: What does 'écouter' mean?
quiz.e: Écouter means 'to listen (to)'.

quiz.q: Choose the correctly conjugated sentence: 'We are working.'
quiz.e: Nous travaillons is the correct nous form of travailler.

quiz.q: Choose the correctly conjugated sentence: 'They are studying.' (masc. group)
quiz.e: Ils étudient — -ent ending, silent.

quiz.q: What is 'vous' form of 'donner'?
quiz.e: Vous donnez — the vous ending is -ez.

quiz.q: Complete: 'Elle ___ la télévision.' (regarder)
quiz.e: Elle regarde — third person singular takes -e.

quiz.q: Which sentence correctly negates 'Il aime le café'?
o: Il aime ne pas le café
Il ne aime le café pas
quiz.e: Il n'aime pas le café is correctly formed with ne...pas around the verb.

quiz.q: What happens to 'ne' before a vowel sound?
o: It is dropped entirely with no replacement
quiz.e: Ne elides to n' before a vowel sound, as in n'aime, n'habite.

quiz.q: Is dropping 'ne' in casual speech considered standard written French?
o: No, both ne and pas are required in standard/written French
No, pas must be dropped instead
quiz.e: Dropping ne is only acceptable in very casual spoken French, not in standard/written French.

quiz.q: What does 'ne...jamais' mean?
quiz.e: Ne...jamais means 'never', following the same pattern as ne...pas.

quiz.q: What does 'ne...plus' mean?
quiz.e: Ne...plus means 'no longer' or 'not anymore'.

quiz.q: Which verb needs a spelling change to preserve its 'soft g' sound in the nous form?
quiz.e: Manger → nous mangeons keeps the soft g sound with the extra e.

quiz.q: What is the tu form of 'jouer'?
quiz.e: Tu joues — tu ending is -es.

quiz.q: Which verb pattern applies to 'adorer' and 'détester'?
quiz.e: Both adorer and détester are regular -er verbs.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I like to dance'?
quiz.e: Aimer + infinitive: j'aime danser.

quiz.q: What is the il/elle form of 'étudier'?
quiz.e: Il/elle étudie — third person singular ending is -e.

quiz.q: Which sentence uses the correct word order for negation with an adverb?
o: Je ne mange pas souvent de viande
Je mange ne pas souvent de viande
Je ne souvent mange pas de viande
quiz.e: Ne...pas wraps the verb; souvent commonly follows: je ne mange pas souvent de viande.

quiz.q: What is the meaning of 'arriver'?
quiz.e: Arriver means 'to arrive', a regular -er verb.

quiz.q: Choose the correct form: 'Tu ___ au parc.' (arriver)
quiz.e: Tu arrives — tu ending is -es.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a regular -er verb (it's irregular)?
quiz.e: Aller (to go) ends in -er but is highly irregular, unlike the other regular verbs listed.

quiz.q: What is the correct 'je' form of 'être'?
quiz.e: Je suis is the irregular je form of être.

quiz.q: What is the correct 'nous' form of 'être'?
quiz.e: Nous sommes is the irregular nous form of être.

quiz.q: What is the correct 'ils' form of 'être'?
quiz.e: Ils/elles sont is the irregular plural form of être.

quiz.q: What is the correct 'j'' form of 'avoir'?
quiz.e: J'ai is the irregular je form of avoir.

quiz.q: What is the correct 'vous' form of 'avoir'?
quiz.e: Vous avez is the irregular vous form of avoir.

quiz.q: What is the correct 'ils' form of 'avoir'?
quiz.e: Ils/elles ont is the irregular plural form of avoir.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I am twenty years old'?
quiz.e: Age uses avoir in French: j'ai vingt ans (literally 'I have twenty years').

quiz.q: What does 'avoir faim' mean?
quiz.e: Avoir faim means 'to be hungry'.

quiz.q: What does 'avoir soif' mean?
quiz.e: Avoir soif means 'to be thirsty'.

quiz.q: What does 'avoir peur' mean?
quiz.e: Avoir peur means 'to be afraid'.

quiz.q: How do you say 'there is a book on the table'?
o: Il y a un livre sur la table
Il est un livre sur la table
Il a un livre sur la table
quiz.e: Il y a is the correct invariable expression for 'there is/are'.

quiz.q: How do you say 'there aren't any books'?
o: Il n'y a pas de livres
Il n'y a pas des livres
Il ne y a pas livres
Il n'y a pas un livres
quiz.e: Negation with il y a: il n'y a pas de + noun (des/un also become de).

quiz.q: Does 'il y a' change form for plural subjects?
quiz.e: Il y a is invariable and never changes, regardless of what follows.

quiz.q: Which is the correctly formed formal question using inversion?
quiz.e: Parles-tu français ? uses verb-subject inversion, the more formal question style.

quiz.q: Which question form is most informal, using only intonation?
o: Est-ce que tu aimes le café ?
quiz.e: Tu aimes le café ? with rising intonation is the casual spoken form.

quiz.q: What word starts a neutral, common way to ask a yes/no question?
quiz.e: Est-ce que + statement is the standard neutral way to form a question.

quiz.q: What is inserted between two vowels during inversion, e.g. 'Parle-t-il ?'
quiz.e: A -t- is inserted for pronunciation when the verb ends in a vowel and the pronoun starts with one: Parle-t-il.

quiz.q: What does 'Où' mean?
quiz.e: Où means 'where'.

quiz.q: What does 'Pourquoi' mean?
quiz.e: Pourquoi means 'why'.

quiz.q: What does 'Combien' mean?
quiz.e: Combien (de) means 'how much/how many'.

quiz.q: What does 'Quel/Quelle' mean, and how does it behave?
quiz.e: Quel agrees in gender/number with the noun: quelle heure, quels livres.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'What are you doing?'
quiz.e: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ? is the standard way to ask 'what are you doing'.

quiz.q: Choose the correct sentence: 'She is a doctor.'
quiz.e: Il/elle est + profession drops the article: elle est docteur.

quiz.q: Choose the correct sentence using c'est.
quiz.e: C'est is followed by an article + noun: c'est un docteur.

quiz.q: What does 'avoir chaud' mean?
quiz.e: Avoir chaud means 'to be hot' (referring to a person feeling warm).

quiz.q: What does 'avoir froid' mean?
quiz.e: Avoir froid means 'to be cold'.

quiz.q: Complete: 'Nous ___ étudiants.' (être)
quiz.e: Nous sommes étudiants — nous form of être.

quiz.q: Complete: 'Ils ___ deux chats.' (avoir)
quiz.e: Ils ont deux chats — ils form of avoir.

quiz.q: Which question word means 'who'?
quiz.e: Qui means 'who'.

quiz.q: How is 'Y a-t-il...?' used?
o: As a formal question form of il y a
quiz.e: Y a-t-il...? is the inverted, formal question form of il y a.

quiz.q: Which sentence correctly uses avoir for a physical state?
quiz.e: J'ai faim (I am hungry) uses avoir, not être or an article.

quiz.q: Why is 'Il est un professeur' considered incorrect?
o: Because no article is used after il/elle est + profession
Because il est only works with adjectives
quiz.e: After il/elle est + profession, no article is used: il est professeur (or c'est un professeur).

quiz.q: What is the tu form of avoir?
quiz.e: Tu as is the tu form of avoir.

quiz.q: What is the tu form of être?
quiz.e: Tu es is the tu form of être.

quiz.q: Choose the correct inversion question with a proper noun subject.
quiz.e: With a noun subject, add a pronoun for inversion: Marie parle-t-elle français ?

quiz.q: What does 'Quand' mean?
quiz.e: Quand means 'when'.

quiz.q: Which sentence means 'What time is it?'
quiz.e: Quelle heure est-il ? uses the feminine form quelle to agree with heure.

quiz.q: Complete correctly: 'Vous ___ vingt ans.' (avoir)
quiz.e: Vous avez vingt ans — vous form of avoir used for age.

quiz.q: Which best explains the difference between il y a and il est?
o: Il y a means 'there is/are'; il est means 'he/it is'
Il y a is only for people
Il est is invariable, il y a isn't
quiz.e: Il y a introduces existence ('there is/are'); il est describes a specific subject.

quiz.q: What is the feminine form of 'grand'?
quiz.e: Add -e for the feminine singular: grande.

quiz.q: What is the feminine form of 'heureux' (happy)?
quiz.e: -eux changes to -euse in the feminine: heureuse.

quiz.q: What is the feminine form of 'actif' (active)?
quiz.e: -f changes to -ve in the feminine: active.

quiz.q: What is the feminine form of 'bon' (good)?
quiz.e: -on doubles the consonant + e in the feminine: bonne.

quiz.q: What is the feminine form of 'beau' (beautiful)?
quiz.e: Beau is irregular in the feminine: belle.

quiz.q: What is the masculine plural of 'petit'?
quiz.e: Add -s for masculine plural: petits.

quiz.q: What is the masculine plural of 'français' (French)?
quiz.e: Adjectives ending in -s don't change in the masculine plural: français stays français.

quiz.q: What is the masculine plural of 'beau' before a noun?
quiz.e: Beau becomes beaux in the masculine plural: de beaux tableaux.

quiz.q: Which adjectives typically come BEFORE the noun?
quiz.e: BAGS adjectives (beauty, age, goodness, size) are a short list placed before the noun.

quiz.q: Where do most French descriptive adjectives go?
o: At the start of the sentence
quiz.e: Most descriptive adjectives, like colors and nationalities, follow the noun.

quiz.q: Choose the correctly placed adjective: 'a big house'
quiz.e: Grand is a BAGS (size) adjective and goes before the noun: une grande maison.

quiz.q: Choose the correctly placed adjective: 'a red car'
quiz.e: Rouge (color) follows the noun: une voiture rouge.

quiz.q: What is the correct form before a vowel-starting masculine noun: 'un ___ homme' (beau)?
quiz.e: Beau becomes bel before a masculine noun starting with a vowel sound: un bel homme.

quiz.q: Which structure is used for 'c'est'?
o: c'est + article + noun, or c'est + adjective (general comment)
quiz.e: C'est is followed by an article+noun or used for a general comment with an adjective.

quiz.q: Which structure is used to describe a specific person already mentioned?
quiz.e: Il/elle est + adjective directly describes someone already known/mentioned: elle est grande.

quiz.q: Choose the correct sentence: 'He is a doctor.'
quiz.e: C'est un docteur is correct: c'est + article + noun.

quiz.q: Choose the correct sentence: 'She is French.'
quiz.e: Nationality after il/elle est has no article: elle est française.

quiz.q: What is the plural form 'ce sont' used for?
quiz.e: Ce sont is the plural version of c'est, used before plural nouns: ce sont mes amis.

quiz.q: What does 'sympathique' mean?
quiz.e: Sympathique means nice or friendly.

quiz.q: What does 'ennuyeux/ennuyeuse' mean?
quiz.e: Ennuyeux/ennuyeuse means boring.

quiz.q: What does 'fatigué(e)' mean?
quiz.e: Fatigué(e) means tired.

quiz.q: Choose the correctly agreed sentence: 'The blue shirts' (chemises, feminine plural)
quiz.e: Bleu agrees in gender and number: les chemises bleues.

quiz.q: Choose the correctly agreed sentence: 'The black shoes' (chaussures, feminine plural)
quiz.e: Noir agrees: les chaussures noires.

quiz.q: What is the feminine form of 'nouveau' (new)?
quiz.e: Nouveau is irregular in the feminine: nouvelle.

quiz.q: What is the feminine form of 'vieux' (old)?
quiz.e: Vieux is irregular in the feminine: vieille.

quiz.q: What is the masculine singular form used before a vowel: 'un ___ arbre' (nouveau, new)?
quiz.e: Nouveau becomes nouvel before a vowel-starting masculine noun: un nouvel arbre.

quiz.q: Choose the correct four-form agreement pattern for 'petit'.
quiz.e: The four forms in order are: masc. sing., fem. sing., masc. pl., fem. pl. — petit, petite, petits, petites.

quiz.q: When a group has mixed genders (some nouns masc., some fem.), which adjective agreement applies?
quiz.e: A mixed-gender group takes the masculine plural adjective by convention.

quiz.q: Choose the correctly ordered phrase: 'a good book'
quiz.e: Bon (goodness, BAGS) precedes the noun: un bon livre.

quiz.q: Choose the correctly ordered phrase: 'an interesting book'
quiz.e: Intéressant is not a BAGS adjective and follows the noun.

quiz.q: What does 'joli(e)' mean?
quiz.e: Joli(e) means pretty.

quiz.q: What does 'gentil/gentille' mean?
quiz.e: Gentil/gentille means kind.

quiz.q: Choose correct: 'c'est ___ idée.' (a good idea, feminine noun)
quiz.e: Une bonne idée — feminine article and adjective agreement.

quiz.q: Choose the correct sentence describing a specific woman: 'She is intelligent.'
quiz.e: Elle est intelligente uses il/elle est + adjective, agreeing in the feminine.

quiz.q: What is the feminine plural of 'joli'?
quiz.e: Jolies is feminine plural: des fleurs jolies (though joli is often placed before, e.g. de jolies fleurs).

quiz.q: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
quiz.e: Une grande maison — grande agrees with feminine maison and precedes it.

quiz.q: What happens to adjectives already ending in -e (masculine) in the feminine form?
quiz.e: Adjectives ending in -e don't change for feminine: un homme rouge → une femme rouge.

quiz.q: Which BAGS category does 'vieux' belong to?
quiz.e: Vieux (old) is an Age adjective from the BAGS group.

quiz.q: Which BAGS category does 'joli' belong to?
quiz.e: Joli (pretty) falls under Beauty.

quiz.q: What does 'le frère' mean?
quiz.e: Le frère means brother.

quiz.q: What does 'la sœur' mean?
quiz.e: La sœur means sister.

quiz.q: What does 'les grands-parents' mean?
quiz.e: Les grands-parents means grandparents.

quiz.q: What does 'le fils' mean?
quiz.e: Le fils means son.

quiz.q: 'La fille' can mean:
o: daughter or girl, depending on context
quiz.e: La fille means both 'girl' and 'daughter'; context clarifies which.

quiz.q: What does 'l'oncle' mean?
quiz.e: L'oncle means uncle.

quiz.q: What does 'la tante' mean?
quiz.e: La tante means aunt.

quiz.q: What does 'le neveu' mean?
quiz.e: Le neveu means nephew.

quiz.q: What does 'la nièce' mean?
quiz.e: La nièce means niece.

quiz.q: What does 'le petit-fils' mean?
quiz.e: Le petit-fils means grandson.

quiz.q: What is 'mon' used for?
o: my, before a masculine noun or feminine vowel-starting noun
quiz.e: Mon is used before masculine nouns and before feminine nouns starting with a vowel sound.

quiz.q: How do you say 'my mother' correctly?
quiz.e: Ma mère — mère is feminine, and doesn't start with a vowel, so ma is correct.

quiz.q: How do you say 'my friend' if 'amie' is feminine and starts with a vowel?
quiz.e: Before a feminine noun starting with a vowel sound, mon replaces ma: mon amie.

quiz.q: What determines the form of a possessive adjective (mon/ma/mes)?
o: The gender and number of the noun possessed
The gender of the person addressed
quiz.e: Possessive adjectives agree with the noun owned, not the owner.

quiz.q: What does 'son père' mean?
o: his father OR her father, depending on context
quiz.e: Son agrees with père (masculine), so 'son père' can mean his or her father — context decides.

quiz.q: What is the plural possessive form 'nos' used for?
quiz.e: Nos is the plural form of notre, used with plural nouns: nos enfants.

quiz.q: What is 'votre' used for?
quiz.e: Votre is used for formal 'your' or plural 'your': votre travail, votre famille.

quiz.q: What does 'leur' mean?
quiz.e: Leur/leurs means 'their'.

quiz.q: How do you say 'their cats' (chats, plural)?
quiz.e: Leurs chats — leurs is the plural form before a plural noun.

quiz.q: How does French express 'Marie's book'?
quiz.e: French has no possessive 's: le livre de Marie (the book of Marie).

quiz.q: How do you say 'the neighbor's dog' correctly (voisin, masculine)?
quiz.e: De + le contracts to du: le chien du voisin.

quiz.q: What does 'C'est le sac de qui ?' mean?
quiz.e: C'est le sac de qui ? asks 'Whose bag is it?'

quiz.q: What does 'le mari' mean?
quiz.e: Le mari means husband.

quiz.q: What does 'la belle-mère' mean?
quiz.e: La belle-mère means mother-in-law or stepmother.

quiz.q: What does 'le beau-père' mean?
quiz.e: Le beau-père means father-in-law or stepfather.

quiz.q: Choose the correct possessive: 'your (formal) house'
quiz.e: Votre maison — formal/plural 'your' with a singular noun.

quiz.q: Choose the correct possessive: 'our children' (enfants, plural)
quiz.e: Nos enfants — nos is used with plural nouns.

quiz.q: What is the correct possessive for 'his sister' if the owner is male?
quiz.e: Sa sœur — sœur is feminine, so sa is used regardless that the owner is male.

quiz.q: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
quiz.e: Mon ami — masculine noun ami takes mon.

quiz.q: What is 'les petits-enfants'?
quiz.e: Les petits-enfants means grandchildren.

quiz.q: How would you say 'my parents' (parents, plural)?
quiz.e: Mes parents — mes is used for any plural noun.

quiz.q: What does 'la cousine' mean?
quiz.e: La cousine means female cousin (le cousin = male cousin).

quiz.q: Choose the correct possessive adjective: 'her school' (école, feminine, vowel-starting)
quiz.e: Son école — before a feminine vowel-starting noun, son replaces sa.

quiz.q: What is the possessive form for 'your' when speaking informally to one friend about their book?
quiz.e: Ton livre — informal singular 'your' with a masculine noun.

quiz.q: Which sentence means 'It's the professor's car'?
quiz.e: De + le contracts to du: la voiture du professeur.

quiz.q: What is the key rule about son/sa/ses that trips up beginners?
o: They can mean his OR her; only context tells you
They agree with the possessor's gender
quiz.e: Son/sa/ses agree with the noun owned, not the possessor, so they can mean either his or her.

quiz.q: What does 'les parents' mean?
quiz.e: Les parents means parents (mother and father).

quiz.q: Choose the correctly agreed phrase: 'my aunts' (tantes, feminine plural)
quiz.e: Mes tantes — mes for any plural noun.

quiz.q: How do you say 'some bread' correctly?
quiz.e: Du pain uses the masculine partitive article for 'some bread'.

quiz.q: How do you say 'some water' correctly?
quiz.e: De l' is used before a vowel-starting noun: de l'eau.

quiz.q: How do you say 'some lemonade' correctly (limonade, feminine)?
quiz.e: De la is the feminine singular partitive article: de la limonade.

quiz.q: How do you say 'some vegetables' correctly (légumes, plural)?
quiz.e: Des is the plural partitive article: des légumes.

quiz.q: What happens to partitive articles in a negative sentence?
quiz.e: After a negation, du/de la/de l'/des all become de or d': je ne mange pas de viande.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I don't eat meat'?
o: Je ne mange pas de la viande
Je ne mange pas de viande
quiz.e: Negation makes the partitive become simply 'de': je ne mange pas de viande.

quiz.q: What is the polite conditional form of 'vouloir' used to order?
quiz.e: Je voudrais (I would like) is more polite than je veux for ordering.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I would like a coffee, please'?
o: Je veux un café, s'il vous plaît
Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît
J'ai un café, s'il vous plaît
Je suis un café, s'il vous plaît
quiz.e: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît is the standard polite ordering phrase.

quiz.q: What is the nous form of 'vouloir'?
quiz.e: Nous voulons is the nous form of vouloir.

quiz.q: What is the ils form of 'vouloir'?
quiz.e: Ils/elles veulent is the plural form of vouloir.

quiz.q: What does a server typically ask when taking your order?
quiz.e: Qu'est-ce que vous prenez ? = What will you have?

quiz.q: What does 'l'addition, s'il vous plaît' mean?
quiz.e: L'addition, s'il vous plaît means 'the check, please'.

quiz.q: What is 'un croissant'?
quiz.e: Un croissant is a crescent-shaped buttery pastry.

quiz.q: What does 'prendre' mean in a café context?
quiz.e: Prendre means 'to take/have', commonly used for ordering food: je prends un café.

quiz.q: What does 'avoir faim' mean?
quiz.e: Avoir faim means to be hungry.

quiz.q: What does 'avoir soif' mean?
quiz.e: Avoir soif means to be thirsty.

quiz.q: What is the correct je form of 'boire' (to drink)?
quiz.e: Je bois is the irregular je form of boire.

quiz.q: What is the nous form of 'boire'?
quiz.e: Nous buvons is the irregular nous form of boire.

quiz.q: What is the ils form of 'boire'?
quiz.e: Ils/elles boivent is the irregular plural form of boire.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I love chocolate' (general like/dislike, definite article)?
quiz.e: With aimer/adorer/détester expressing general preference, use the definite article: j'adore le chocolat.

quiz.q: What is the correct phrase for 'at the bakery'?
quiz.e: À la boulangerie — feminine noun, à la doesn't contract.

quiz.q: What does 'le petit-déjeuner' mean?
quiz.e: Le petit-déjeuner means breakfast.

quiz.q: What does 'le déjeuner' mean?
quiz.e: Le déjeuner means lunch.

quiz.q: What does 'le dîner' mean?
quiz.e: Le dîner means dinner.

quiz.q: What does 'sucré' mean?
quiz.e: Sucré means sweet.

quiz.q: What does 'salé' mean?
quiz.e: Salé means salty or savory.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'How much is it?'
quiz.e: C'est combien ? asks how much something costs.

quiz.q: Choose the correct negative sentence: 'I don't drink coffee.'
o: Je ne bois pas de café
Je ne bois pas du café
Je ne bois pas le café
quiz.e: After negation, partitive becomes de: je ne bois pas de café.

quiz.q: What does 'les œufs' mean?
quiz.e: Les œufs means eggs.

quiz.q: What does 'le poisson' mean?
quiz.e: Le poisson means fish.

quiz.q: Which verb family does 'manger' belong to?
quiz.e: Manger is a regular -er verb, with a spelling change in the nous form (mangeons).

quiz.q: What is the correct polite phrase to use with a waiter you don't know?
quiz.e: S'il vous plaît is the formal 'please', appropriate with a stranger like a waiter.

quiz.q: What does 'une tarte' refer to?
quiz.e: Une tarte is a pie or tart, a classic bakery item.

quiz.q: How would you say 'some eggs' correctly?
quiz.e: Des œufs — plural partitive article used with a plural noun.

quiz.q: What does 'je préfère le thé' mean?
quiz.e: Je préfère le thé means 'I prefer tea'.

quiz.q: What does 'délicieux/délicieuse' mean?
quiz.e: Délicieux/délicieuse means delicious.

quiz.q: Which is the correct way to say 'at the restaurant'?
quiz.e: Au restaurant — à + le contracts to au before the masculine noun restaurant.

quiz.q: What is the meaning of 'je prends un café crème'?
o: I make a coffee with cream
I'll have a coffee with cream
quiz.e: Je prends un café crème means 'I'll have a coffee with cream'.

quiz.q: What does 'la banque' mean?
quiz.e: La banque means bank.

quiz.q: What does 'la boulangerie' mean?
quiz.e: La boulangerie means bakery.

quiz.q: What does 'la gare' mean?
quiz.e: La gare means train station.

quiz.q: What does 'la bibliothèque' mean?
quiz.e: La bibliothèque means library.

quiz.q: What does 'l'hôpital' mean?
quiz.e: L'hôpital means hospital.

quiz.q: What is the correct je form of 'aller'?
quiz.e: Je vais is the irregular je form of aller.

quiz.q: What is the nous form of 'aller'?
quiz.e: Nous allons is the nous form of aller.

quiz.q: What is the ils form of 'aller'?
quiz.e: Ils/elles vont is the plural form of aller.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I am going to the park' (parc, masculine)?
quiz.e: À + le contracts to au: je vais au parc.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I am going to the bank' (banque, feminine)?
quiz.e: À la banque — feminine noun, à la doesn't contract.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I am going to school' (école, feminine, vowel-starting)?
quiz.e: À l'école — à l' is used before a vowel-starting noun.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I am going to the restrooms' (les toilettes, plural)?
quiz.e: À + les contracts to aux: je vais aux toilettes.

quiz.q: What does 'à côté de' mean?
quiz.e: À côté de means next to.

quiz.q: What does 'en face de' mean?
quiz.e: En face de means across from.

quiz.q: What does 'près de' mean?
quiz.e: Près de means near.

quiz.q: What does 'loin de' mean?
quiz.e: Loin de means far from.

quiz.q: What does 'devant' mean?
quiz.e: Devant means in front of.

quiz.q: What does 'derrière' mean?
quiz.e: Derrière means behind.

quiz.q: What does 'entre' mean?
quiz.e: Entre means between.

quiz.q: How do you say 'next to the park' correctly (parc, masculine)?
quiz.e: De + le contracts to du even inside longer prepositions: à côté du parc.

quiz.q: How do you say 'near the stores' (magasins, plural)?
quiz.e: De + les contracts to des: près des magasins.

quiz.q: What does 'tout droit' mean?
quiz.e: Tout droit means straight ahead, not related to 'right' despite droit's other meaning.

quiz.q: What does 'à droite' mean?
quiz.e: À droite means to the right.

quiz.q: What does 'à gauche' mean?
quiz.e: À gauche means to the left.

quiz.q: How do you politely ask for directions?
o: Pour aller à..., s'il vous plaît ?
quiz.e: Pour aller à..., s'il vous plaît ? = How do I get to..., please?

quiz.q: Which verb form is used for polite direction-giving commands?
quiz.e: Direction-giving typically uses the vous-form imperative: tournez, continuez.

quiz.q: What does 'tournez à droite' mean?
quiz.e: Tournez à droite means turn right.

quiz.q: What does 'continuez tout droit' mean?
quiz.e: Continuez tout droit means continue straight ahead.

quiz.q: What does 'Où est...?' mean?
quiz.e: Où est...? means 'Where is...?'

quiz.q: How do you say 'by bus'?
quiz.e: En bus means by bus.

quiz.q: How do you say 'on foot'?
quiz.e: À pied means on foot.

quiz.q: How do you say 'by bike'?
quiz.e: À vélo means by bike.

quiz.q: How do you say 'by car'?
quiz.e: En voiture means by car.

quiz.q: What does 'C'est loin ?' mean?
quiz.e: C'est loin ? asks 'Is it far?'

quiz.q: What does 'Il faut tourner à gauche' mean?
quiz.e: Il faut + infinitive means 'it's necessary to/you have to': il faut tourner à gauche.

quiz.q: What does 'au coin de la rue' mean?
o: in the middle of the street
at the corner of the street
at the end of the street
quiz.e: Au coin de la rue means at the corner of the street.

quiz.q: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
quiz.e: Je vais au musée — à + le contracts to au before the masculine noun musée.

quiz.q: What does 'prendre le métro' mean?
quiz.e: Prendre le métro means to take the subway.

the (masc. sing. / fem. sing. / plural) — definite articles agreeing with the noun.
a, an, some (masc. sing. / fem. sing. / plural) — indefinite articles.
every noun has a gender that must be memorized with the word, e.g. le livre, la table.
required contraction: je vais au cinéma, never 'à le cinéma'.
required contraction: le livre du professeur, never 'de le professeur'.
plural contractions of à+les and de+les.
never contract, unlike au and aux.
most nouns add -s for plural (silent): le livre → les livres.

un/une/des become de/d' in a negative sentence: je n'ai pas de chien.
to speak — regular -er verb: je parle, nous parlons, ils parlent.
the six present-tense endings for -er verbs, attached to the infinitive stem.
the basic negation structure wrapped around the conjugated verb: je ne parle pas.
spelling-change verb: keeps an extra -e before -ons to preserve the soft g sound.

adds a grave accent in all forms except nous/vous.
aimer followed directly by an infinitive: j'aime danser (I like to dance).

there is / there are — invariable, built from il + y + a.
there isn't/aren't any — negative of il y a.
neutral way to form a yes/no question by adding this phrase before a statement.
formal question form: verb and subject pronoun swap and hyphenate.
c'est + article + noun; il/elle est + adjective or bare profession/nationality.

which/what — agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies.
big/tall — regular adjective agreement pattern, and a BAGS adjective (placed before the noun).
beautiful — irregular; bel is used before a masc. vowel-starting noun (un bel homme).

c'est + article + noun (c'est un livre); il/elle est + adjective/profession without article.
happy — -eux adjectives change to -euse in the feminine.
active — -f adjectives change to -ve in the feminine.
good — -on adjectives double the consonant + e in the feminine, and bon is a BAGS adjective.
nice/friendly / kind — common personality adjectives.
a red car — colors and most descriptive adjectives follow the noun.
new, old — irregular BAGS adjectives with special pre-vowel forms (nouvel, vieil).

brother / sister.
son / daughter (la fille also means 'girl').

his/her/its — agrees with the noun owned; can mean 'his' OR 'her' depending on context.

father-in-law or stepfather / mother-in-law or stepmother.

The check, please.

to be hungry / to be thirsty.

flashcards.d: breakfast / lunch / dinner.

PART_A.q: Which greeting means 'good evening' and is used after dark?
PART_A.e: Bonsoir replaces bonjour once it gets dark.

PART_A.q: What is the informal singular word for 'you', used with friends and family?
PART_A.e: Tu is the informal singular 'you'.

PART_A.q: How is the letter 'H' pronounced/treated at the start of a French word like 'hôtel'?
PART_A.e: H is always silent at the start of a French word.

PART_A.q: What does the cédille in 'français' do?
o: Makes c sound like 's' before a, o, u
PART_A.e: The cédille (ç) gives c an 's' sound before a, o, u.

PART_A.q: How do you write the number 16 in French?
PART_A.e: 16 is the irregular standalone form 'seize'.

PART_A.q: What is the correct definite article for 'chaise' (chair, feminine)?
PART_A.e: La is the feminine singular definite article: la chaise.

PART_A.q: Which article is required before a plural noun such as 'livres' when it's non-specific ('some books')?
PART_A.e: Des is the plural indefinite article, meaning 'some'.

PART_A.q: What is the plural of 'le bureau' (desk)?
PART_A.e: Nouns ending in -eau add -x in the plural: les bureaux.

PART_A.q: Complete: 'Je parle ___ étudiants.' (à + les)
PART_A.e: À + les contracts to aux.

PART_A.q: What happens to 'un/une/des' after a negation like 'je n'ai pas...'?
PART_A.e: After negation, indefinite/partitive articles become de/d': je n'ai pas de chien.

PART_A.q: What is the correct 'vous' form of 'parler'?
PART_A.e: Vous parlez — the vous ending is -ez.

PART_A.q: Which -er verb ending is silent when spoken?
o: -er infinitive marker only, endings are always heard
PART_A.e: The ils/elles ending -ent is silent: 'ils parlent' sounds like 'il parle'.

PART_A.q: What is the correct nous form of 'manger' (to eat)?
PART_A.e: Manger adds an extra -e before -ons to keep the soft g sound.

PART_A.q: How do you correctly negate 'il aime' (he likes)?
PART_A.e: Ne elides to n' before a vowel sound: il n'aime pas.

PART_A.q: What is the correct je form of 'appeler' (to call)?
PART_A.e: Appeler doubles the l in most forms: j'appelle.

PART_A.q: What is the correct 'nous' form of être?
PART_A.e: Nous sommes is the irregular nous form of être.

PART_A.q: How do you say 'I am twenty years old' in French?
PART_A.e: Age uses avoir, not être: j'ai vingt ans.

PART_A.q: What is the correct negative form of 'il y a des livres'?
o: il n'y a pas de livres
il n'y a pas des livres
il y a ne pas livres
il ne y a pas livres
PART_A.e: Negative il y a expressions use de: il n'y a pas de livres.

PART_A.q: Which question word means 'where'?
PART_A.e: Où means 'where'.

PART_A.q: What must be inserted between two vowels in an inverted question like 'Parle...il?'
PART_A.e: A -t- is inserted for pronunciation: Parle-t-il ?

PART_A.q: What is the feminine form of the adjective 'heureux' (happy)?
PART_A.e: -eux becomes -euse in the feminine: heureux → heureuse.

PART_A.q: Which category of adjectives typically comes BEFORE the noun (BAGS)?
o: All adjectives come before the noun
PART_A.e: BAGS = Beauty, Age, Goodness, Size adjectives precede the noun.

PART_A.q: Choose the correctly formed phrase for 'a big house' (grand is BAGS).
PART_A.e: Grand is a BAGS adjective placed before the noun and agrees in gender: une grande maison.

PART_A.q: Which structure is correct for describing a profession: 'She is a doctor'?
PART_A.e: Il/elle est + profession drops the article: elle est docteur.

PART_A.q: What does 'la sœur' mean?
PART_A.e: La sœur means sister.

PART_A.q: Which possessive adjective is used before a feminine noun starting with a vowel, like 'amie'?
PART_A.e: Mon (not ma) is used before a feminine vowel-starting noun: mon amie.

PART_A.q: How do you say 'Marie's book' in French, since there's no possessive 's?
PART_A.e: French restructures with de: le livre de Marie.

PART_A.q: Which article expresses 'some bread' (uncountable) in 'je mange ___ pain'?
PART_A.e: Du is the partitive article before a masculine noun: du pain.

PART_A.q: What is the polite conditional form of 'vouloir' used to order at a café?
PART_A.e: Je voudrais (I would like) is the polite way to order.

PART_A.q: What is the correct form for 'I am going to the museum' (le musée)?
PART_A.e: À + le contracts to au: je vais au musée.

PART_B1.q: Which of these responses correctly answers 'Comment allez-vous ?'
PART_B1.e: Ça va bien, merci answers how you are doing.

PART_B1.q: What is the difference in meaning between 'a' and 'à'?
PART_B1.e: 'a' comes from avoir (has); 'à' is the preposition to/at.

PART_B1.q: Which noun ending pattern is almost always feminine?
PART_B1.e: Nouns ending in -tion are almost always feminine, e.g. la nation.

PART_B1.q: What is the plural of 'le journal' (newspaper)?
PART_B1.e: Most -al nouns change to -aux in the plural: les journaux.

PART_B1.q: Does 'à + la' ever contract?
PART_B1.e: À la and à l' never contract, unlike à le and à les.

PART_B1.q: What is the correct nous form of 'commencer' (to begin)?
PART_B1.e: Commencer changes c to ç before -ons: nous commençons.

PART_B1.q: What is the correct je form of 'préférer' (to prefer)?
PART_B1.e: Préférer changes é to è in most forms: je préfère.

PART_B1.q: How many English meanings can the single form 'je parle' express?
o: Three: 'I speak', 'I am speaking', 'I do speak'
PART_B1.e: French present tense covers simple, progressive, and emphatic meanings.

PART_B1.q: What is the correct 'ils/elles' form of avoir?
PART_B1.e: Ils/elles ont is the irregular plural form of avoir.

PART_B1.q: Which avoir expression means 'to be hungry'?
PART_B1.e: Avoir faim literally means 'to have hunger', i.e. to be hungry.

PART_B1.q: Which is the neutral, commonly used way to form a yes/no question?
PART_B1.e: Est-ce que + statement is the neutral, widely used question form.

PART_B1.q: What is the irregular feminine form of 'beau' (beautiful)?
PART_B1.e: Beau → belle is an irregular feminine form that must be memorized.

PART_B1.q: Which sentence correctly uses c'est vs il est for a profession?
PART_B1.e: Il est + profession drops the article: il est médecin.

PART_B1.q: What is the masculine plural form of 'petit' (small)?
PART_B1.e: Petit → petits adds -s for the masculine plural.

PART_B1.q: What does 'le beau-père' mean?
PART_B1.e: Le beau-père means father-in-law or stepfather.

PART_B1.q: Can 'son père' mean both 'his father' and 'her father'?
PART_B1.e: Son/sa/ses agree with the noun owned, not the owner, so son père can mean his or her father.

PART_B1.q: Which verb is irregular and means 'to drink', conjugated as 'je bois, nous buvons'?
PART_B1.e: Boire (to drink) is irregular: je bois, nous buvons, ils boivent.

PART_B1.q: What happens to the partitive article in a negative sentence like 'je ne mange pas ___ fromage'?
PART_B1.e: Partitive articles collapse to de/d' after a negation: je ne mange pas de fromage.

PART_B1.q: What is the correct 'je' form of aller (to go)?
PART_B1.e: Je vais is the irregular je form of aller.

PART_B1.q: What is the correct contraction in 'à côté ___ parc' (next to the park)?
PART_B1.e: De + le contracts to du even inside longer prepositions: à côté du parc.

PART_B2.q: Which accent appears in 'mère' and 'fête', giving an open 'eh' sound?
PART_B2.e: È and ê both give an open sound; mère uses è, fête uses ê.

PART_B2.q: Which sentence correctly expresses 'I have some apples' in French?
PART_B2.e: French requires the plural indefinite article des even though English can drop 'some'.

PART_B2.q: What is the correct je form of 'acheter' (to buy)?
PART_B2.e: Acheter takes a grave accent in most forms except nous/vous: j'achète.

PART_B2.q: Which structure means 'there is/there are' and never changes form?
PART_B2.e: Il y a is invariable regardless of singular or plural: il y a un livre / il y a des livres.

PART_B2.q: Which special masculine singular form of 'beau' is used before a vowel-starting noun, as in 'a handsome man'?
PART_B2.e: Beau becomes bel before a masculine noun starting with a vowel sound: un bel homme.

PART_B2.q: What is the correct possessive for 'our children' (les enfants, plural)?
PART_B2.e: Nos is the plural possessive form of notre, used for any plural noun.

PART_B2.q: What is the correct way to politely ask for the check at a restaurant?
PART_B2.e: L'addition, s'il vous plaît is the standard polite request for the check.

PART_B2.q: Which imperative form is used to give directions politely to a stranger (vous-form)?
PART_B2.e: Direction-giving uses the vous-form imperative by default with strangers: tournez.

PART_B2.q: What does 'Il faut tourner à gauche' mean?
o: It is forbidden to turn left
PART_B2.e: Il faut + infinitive means 'it is necessary to' / 'you have to'.

PART_B2.q: What is the correct definite article for 'hôtel' (masculine, silent h, vowel sound)?
PART_B2.e: L' is used because the silent h makes hôtel start with a vowel sound.

PART_C.q: Written response: choose TWO concepts from different units and construct an argument connecting them. Cite specific evidence from each.
o: Names both concepts precisely, gives concrete evidence for each, and explains the causal/logical bridge
Lists the two topics without connecting them
Describes only one concept in detail
Gives a personal opinion with no course evidence
PART_C.e: Strong responses anchor every claim in specific unit content.

PART_C.q: Essay plan: identify the single most important takeaway of this course. Defend it using three units as evidence, then address one counterargument.
o: Clear thesis, three unit-specific pieces of evidence, genuine counterargument, resolution
PART_C.e: Full argumentative architecture earns top marks.
